image.subject: A woman in her thirties with shoulder-length brown hair and a cardigan, sitting across a desk from a colleague, looking straight at him with a steady, honest expression

storyboard.claim: Own the failure face to face: check your ego and admit you don't know what went wrong.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A manager sits across a desk and holds eye contact with a colleague.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Opens the honesty passage with a concrete action after the abstract coachability claim.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the physical posture of candour, which the narration describes but does not picture.

storyboard.claim: The sentence a leader must be willing to say out loud: I don't know what went wrong.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only quotation card with the spoken line.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the spoken script the manager delivers.
storyboard.addedInformation: The exact words to say, which no photograph could carry.

image.subject: A polished executive in a dark suit at a glass-walled office table, one hand raised in a practised, reassuring gesture while a colleague looks unconvinced

storyboard.claim: Rather than dancing around the truth with corporate spin, be direct.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An executive performing reassurance at a table while a colleague is not convinced.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Follows the manager's admission with the contrast of corporate spin.
storyboard.addedInformation: Makes the spin visible as a performance.

image.subject: A stocky white-haired man in his sixties, warm and direct, wearing a plain open-collar shirt and a sport jacket, standing at the head of a long conference table with his hands open, speaking to a team of colleagues

storyboard.claim: Humility means serving something larger than your own career, the company and the team.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Bill Campbell leads a meeting from the head of a conference table.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains humility as service after the spin contrast.
storyboard.addedInformation: Puts the coach physically at the head of the team he serves.

image.subject: A glass-walled Silicon Valley office with a long conference table and whiteboards, the room empty except for a single chair pulled out at the table

storyboard.claim: Campbell's true product was trust, and the narration frames the honesty that makes it.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An empty glass-walled office with a long table, a place where trust gets built.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns from humility to the product Campbell was really selling.
storyboard.addedInformation: Places the abstract idea of trust in a concrete workplace.

storyboard.claim: Trust is manufactured from honesty and humility.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A checklist of the raw materials of trust.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Lists the inputs the previous beat named.
storyboard.addedInformation: Makes the formula scannable for a muted viewer.

image.subject: A confident executive in a dark suit at a conference room lectern, delivering a polished presentation with a fixed smile while a row of audience members looks on guardedly

storyboard.claim: You cannot build trust with someone who is constantly performing and hiding flaws.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An executive performing polish at a lectern before a guarded audience.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains why the honesty raw materials matter, by showing their opposite.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows performance as a visible posture, not just an idea.

image.subject: A small team of colleagues gathered around a whiteboard covered in diagrams in a bright glass-walled office, one person pointing at a diagram

storyboard.claim: Once trust is built, the coachable team needs rigorous decision-making processes.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A team at a whiteboard working through a decision process.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Moves from building trust to assembling the team that uses it.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the process as shared work at a board.

storyboard.claim: How does this team actually perform when an existential crisis hits?
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only question card.
storyboard.onScreenText: HOW DOES THE TEAM PERFORM IN A CRISIS?
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns from the team to the test it faces.
storyboard.addedInformation: The question frames the case study that follows.

image.subject: A dim glass-walled office late at night, the only light coming from a single desk lamp over a stack of papers and a ringing phone

storyboard.claim: The ultimate stress test is pressure dialed to the absolute maximum.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A late-night office under pressure, a ringing phone on the desk.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the question with the setting of pressure.
storyboard.addedInformation: Gives the pressure a time and place.

image.subject: A slim man in his forties with a black mock turtleneck, jeans and sneakers, standing at a tall glass office window with his arms crossed, intense focused gaze

storyboard.claim: In 2010 Apple sues Google over Android.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Steve Jobs stands at a glass office window with his arms crossed.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Opens the case study with the dispute's date and parties.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the year and the Apple side visually.

image.subject: A pair of chairs facing each other across a small wooden table in a quiet office corner, one chair pushed back as if a conversation just ended

storyboard.claim: This is not a standard patent dispute; it is painfully personal.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Two empty chairs facing each other after a difficult conversation.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shifts from the dispute to its emotional weight.
storyboard.addedInformation: Makes the personal rupture visible through the chairs.

left.label: APPLE
left.subject: A slim man in his forties with a black mock turtleneck, jeans and sneakers, seated at a desk with a serious, betrayed look

right.label: GOOGLE
right.subject: A young man in his late twenties with tousled brown hair and a casual sweater, standing at a desk with a phone in his hand, thoughtful expression

storyboard.claim: Jobs feels betrayed by Google entering the phone market.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Side-by-side: Jobs seated and wounded, Page holding a phone.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Sets the two sides of the rupture against each other.
storyboard.addedInformation: The phone is the object of the betrayal, shown on the Google side.

image.subject: A stocky white-haired man in his sixties, warm and direct, wearing a plain open-collar shirt and a sport jacket, standing alone between two empty chairs in a glass-walled office, looking tense

storyboard.claim: Bill Campbell is caught in the middle: friend to Jobs, adviser to Apple, mentor to Google.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Campbell standing between two empty chairs, caught in the middle.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Places Campbell in the middle of the two sides from the compare.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows his three roles as a position, not a list.

image.subject: A man in his fifties with short graying hair and a dark blazer over an open-collar shirt, leaning across a desk toward a stocky white-haired man in a sport jacket, speaking urgently

storyboard.claim: Eric Schmidt brings Bill the absolute legal and business problem.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Schmidt leans across a desk toward Campbell with an urgent face.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Brings the problem to Campbell, who is in the middle.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the urgency of the request in the body language.

image.subject: A cluttered executive desk with patent folders, a stack of legal briefs and a open laptop showing dense text, a legal pad covered with notes

storyboard.claim: A CEO's instinct is to dive into the patents, the briefs and the lawyers.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A desk piled with patents, briefs and notes.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Describes the expected reaction Campbell does not have.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the detailed work the instinct would begin with.

image.subject: A closed stack of unread legal briefs sitting untouched on a clean glass office table, with a single pen placed neatly beside them

storyboard.claim: Campbell does not read a single patent or legal brief.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A closed stack of briefs left untouched on a clean table.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows what Campbell does not do, in contrast with the instinct.
storyboard.addedInformation: Makes the refusal to dive in a visible, untouched object.

design.kicker: PUT THE RIGHT PERSON IN CHARGE

image.subject: A stocky white-haired man in his sixties, warm and direct, wearing a plain open-collar shirt and a sport jacket, pointing decisively across a conference table toward a colleague who is listening

storyboard.claim: Campbell tells Schmidt to put Alan Eustace in charge of diplomacy between the two companies.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Campbell points across the table, directing the assignment.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the concrete action that replaces diving into details.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the decision as a gesture of delegation.

image.subject: A pair of hands moving a single chessboard piece to a new square on a glass-topped office table, with a folder of papers pushed aside

storyboard.claim: Skipping the details is the operational pivot of a master manager.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A hand moves one piece while papers are pushed aside.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains why the delegation is a move, not an abdication.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows strategic repositioning as a single decisive move.

storyboard.claim: The first panicked instinct is to ask how to solve the problem.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only question card.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the instinct the previous beats said to resist.
storyboard.addedInformation: The question is the one the reader is asked to stop asking.

image.subject: A manager in a cardigan with a hand raised toward her own face, pausing mid-thought at her desk, a closed notebook in front of her

storyboard.claim: You have to train yourself to stop before fixing.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A manager pauses with a hand raised, halting an impulse.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns the question into the act of stopping.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the pause as a physical act.

image.subject: A cluster of engineers leaning in together around one laptop at a workstation, two monitors glowing behind them, all talking at once

storyboard.claim: The correct question is who the right team is, not how to solve it.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Engineers gather around a laptop to work out the problem together.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the replacement question a picture of a team.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows a team forming around the problem.

image.subject: A bright open office with a small group of colleagues seated together at a long table, facing one another rather than a single leader

storyboard.claim: You work with the team, not the problem.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A group seated around a table facing one another.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: States the principle the team picture illustrated.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the layout of equal peers.

image.subject: A group of six young associate product managers in an open Silicon Valley office, gathered around a table with laptops and notebooks, deep in a heated discussion

storyboard.claim: The associate product managers at Google are a group of very sharp young people.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Six young product associates at a table in a meeting.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces the group in the example of the principle.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the size and youth of the group.

image.subject: Young associates slumped over a table covered in printed forms and a tangle of sticky notes, looking frustrated

storyboard.claim: The group is stuck on minor bureaucratic problems and technical roadblocks.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Frustrated young associates over paper forms and sticky notes.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Describes the group's complaints from the previous beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: Makes the minor obstacles look heavy.

image.subject: A woman in her thirties with shoulder-length brown hair and a cardigan, leaning over a colleague's laptop and reaching to take the keyboard, a confident look on her face

storyboard.claim: Marissa's instinct is to jump in and fix their problems herself.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A manager reaches over and takes the keyboard from a colleague.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the instinct the APM group's complaints provoke.
storyboard.addedInformation: The keyboard grab shows the takeover as an action.

image.subject: A stocky white-haired man in his sixties, warm and direct, wearing a plain open-collar shirt and a sport jacket, speaking quietly with a hand on the wall of a bright corridor

storyboard.claim: Bill observes and pulls her aside to speak privately.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Campbell speaks quietly in a corridor.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Moves from the instinct to Campbell's intervention.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the private, one-to-one setting of the advice.

storyboard.claim: Campbell tells her she is entirely the wrong person to help them.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only statement.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Delivers the counterintuitive verdict the aside led to.
storyboard.addedInformation: Sets up the reasons in the next beat.

image.subject: A corner office with a large desk and a high-backed leather chair, empty, seen from the doorway of a room where junior staff sit at small tables

storyboard.claim: She is their boss and knows the answer, but has too much institutional power.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A large corner office looking over smaller desks.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains why she is the wrong person.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the power gap as a physical distance.

image.subject: Two young professionals sitting together at a bright table with a whiteboard, a clear space at the head of the table left unoccupied

storyboard.claim: She should create a peer forum where the APMs can meet without her.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Peers at a table with the head seat left empty.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the remedy for the power problem.
storyboard.addedInformation: The empty head of the table shows the manager stepping back.

image.subject: A circle of young professionals in folding chairs in a bright office, leaning in and speaking openly to one another, no manager at the center

storyboard.claim: The forum forces peer-to-peer vulnerability.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A circle of peers speaking openly.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains the effect of the peer forum.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the vulnerability as a circle with no authority at its center.

image.subject: A whiteboard covered in notes beside a young team tapping their own laptops and working out the next steps together, no manager hovering nearby

storyboard.claim: The team builds its own capacity instead of waiting for answers from a vending machine.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A team working through next steps at a whiteboard without a manager.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Contrasts self-solving with the vending machine the manager would have been.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the team solving on its own.

storyboard.claim: Banter that connects back to the burning building analogy from earlier.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only statement.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Hosts transition between speakers.
storyboard.addedInformation: None beyond the callback.

storyboard.claim: Let's push back on the optics of this tactic.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only question card.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Opens the counterargument.
storyboard.addedInformation: Frames the objection the next beats answer.

image.subject: A manager at a glass office table with arms folded, looking past an empty chair while a team works in the background

storyboard.claim: If the team is failing and the leader delegates without looking at details, it looks like passing the buck.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A manager with folded arms, distant from a working team.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: States the objection in concrete terms.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the detachment the objection warns about.

storyboard.claim: Passing the buck is what it looks like.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only punchline.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Lands the objection.
storyboard.addedInformation: None beyond the phrase.

image.subject: A leader in shirtsleeves rolling up sleeves at an engineer's desk, leaning in to a monitor with colleagues gathered around, a visible wish to be part of the work

storyboard.claim: Getting in the trenches is a common misconception of good leadership.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A leader rolls up sleeves to join the work at a desk.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the counter-view a face.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the misconception as a sincere, human impulse.

image.subject: A coiled red fire hose mounted on the wall of a glass-walled office corridor, with a closed door at the end

storyboard.claim: Grabbing the fire hose at executive level is micromanaging the fire.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A fire hose on a corridor wall, unused.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the metaphor a literal object.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the metaphor's tool without any fire or harm.

storyboard.claim: If you keep jumping into technical trenches, you abandon your actual job, which is what?
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only question card.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Asks the question the next beat answers.
storyboard.addedInformation: Sets up the answer.

storyboard.claim: The job is managing the ecosystem: assess the fire chief, provide water pressure and resources, manage the perimeter.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only list of three responsibilities.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the question with a list.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the three duties of the leader in the metaphor.
